1.note: The author is using the words **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:46. Alternate translation: [that David defeated the Philistines]

Here and frequently in this chapter, the author uses **David**, one person who was involved in the actions he describes, to represent everyone who was involved. Alternate translation: [David and his soldiers]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:23. Alternate translation: [and in the surrounding villages]

Here, **hand** represents possession or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the possession of the Philistines]

2.note: The author is referring to members of a people group by the name of their ancestor. Alternate translation: [And he defeated the Moabite army, and the Moabites became servants]

The author is using the first thing that subject peoples would do to deliver tribute, lift it onto the backs of animals that would transport it, to represent the entire action of paying tribute. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 6. Alternate translation: [bringers of tribute] or [vassals]

3.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Hadadezer. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when Hadadezer went]
See the Introduction to this chapter for a discussion of this phrase and for suggestions of how you might represent it in your translation.

**Euphrates** is the modern name of this river. The Hebrew text calls it by its ancient name, “the River of Perath.” Some versions of the Bible use that name. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the name that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the name that the ULT uses.

4.q: וַ⁠יְעַקֵּ֤ר דָּוִיד֙ אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠רֶ֔כֶב וַ⁠יּוֹתֵ֥ר מִמֶּ֖⁠נּוּ מֵ֥אָה רָֽכֶב
4.note: Here the term **chariots** represents the horses that pulled these chariots. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And David hamstrung all of the chariot horses, but he left from them 100 horses]

4.q: וַ⁠יְעַקֵּ֤ר דָּוִיד֙ אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠רֶ֔כֶב וַ⁠יּוֹתֵ֥ר מִמֶּ֖⁠נּוּ מֵ֥אָה רָֽכֶב
4.note: If, in your language, it would appear that the author was making a statement here and then contradicting it, you could reverse the order of the clauses so that the exception is stated first and then the larger group is named second. Alternate translation: [And after choosing 100 horses from the chariots, David had his soldiers hamstring the rest]

When the author says that David **hamstrung** these horses, he meant that he had his soldiers use a method of disabling them by cutting tendons in their legs. This would be done carefully so that horses would still be able to walk and carry loads, but they would no longer be able to run. As a result, they could no longer be used in warfare. If your readers would not be familiar with what hamstringing is, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [And David had his soldiers disable all of the chariot horses by cutting their leg tendons]

5.note: Here, **Aram of Damascus** represents the army of the Aramean kingdom whose capital was Damascus. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the army of the Aramean kingdom whose capital was Damascus]
See how you translated the term “struck” in the similar context in 4:43. Alternate translation: [And David and his soldiers killed]

6.note: The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 8:6 reads “And David put garrisons.” The term “garrisons” may have dropped out here in the process of copying, or the author may be leaving it to be understood. (However, he states it explicitly in verse 13.) You can supply this word if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And David put garrisons]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:2. Alternate translation: [and the Arameans became servants to David]

6.q: וַ⁠יּ֤וֹשַׁע יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠דָוִ֔יד בְּ⁠כֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלָֽךְ
6.note: The author is making a summary comment about everything he has described since introducing a new event in [8:1](ta:08). This signals the end of his account of these wars that David fought. Use the natural form in your language for indicating the conclusion of a story.

7.q: אֵ֚ת שִׁלְטֵ֣י הַ⁠זָּהָ֔ב אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָי֔וּ עַ֖ל עַבְדֵ֣י הֲדַדְעָ֑זֶר
7.note: The meaning of the word translated as **shields** is uncertain. It could be a general term for military equipment whose meaning must be understood from the context. In some contexts, such as Jeremiah 51:11, it seems to mean “quivers” or arrow-cases, and some versions also translate it that way here. However, the context seems to support the meaning of **shields**. Some ancient rulers had their bodyguard carry shields that were plated with precious metals, and Hadadezer may have done that. Alternate translation: [the gold-plated shields that Hadadezer’s bodyguard had carried]

8.note: The author calls this city **Tibhath**, but in the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 8:8, it is called “Betah.” It appears possible that at some point in the process of transmission, scribes transposed two of the letters in this name. However, this is not certain, and it is not clear which may have been the original form. So we do not recommend that you change the name either here or in 2 Samuel so that it is the same in both places. Instead, if it would be helpful to your readers, you may wish to note the difference in a footnote.

9.note: To translate the term **struck** here and in the next verse, see how you translated it in the similar context in [18:1](ta:18). Alternate translation: [David had defeated]

10.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֣ח אֶת־הֲדֽוֹרָם־בְּנ֣⁠וֹ אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ־דָּ֠וִיד ל⁠שאול־ל֨⁠וֹ לְ⁠שָׁל֜וֹם וּֽ⁠לְ⁠בָרֲכ֗⁠וֹ עַל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר נִלְחַ֤ם בַּ⁠הֲדַדְעֶ֨זֶר֙ וַ⁠יַּכֵּ֔⁠הוּ
10.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because King David had fought with Hadadezer and had struck him, he sent Hadoram his son to him to ask him for peace and to bless him]

**Hadoram** is a variant spelling of the name “Joram,” which occurs in the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 8:10. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where it appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Joram]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Here the word **peace** indicates the idea of “welfare.” Alternate translation: [for peaceful relations] or [to make a peace treaty]

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what is happening in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The author is using **a man of war** as a common expression of his culture to mean “someone who fought wars against.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For Hadadezer had been fighting wars against Toi]

The author assumes that readers will understand that **Hadoram** brought these **vessels** to David from his father Tou as a gift. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 8:10 states this directly.You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And all of the vessels of gold and silver and bronze that Hadoram brought to him from his father Tou]

11.note: See how you translated the expression “the sons of” in the similar context in 1:43. Alternate translation: [and from the Ammonites]

12.q: וְ⁠אַבְשַׁ֣י בֶּן־צְרוּיָ֗ה הִכָּ֤ה אֶת־אֱדוֹם֙ בְּ⁠גֵ֣יא הַמֶּ֔לַח שְׁמוֹנָ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר אָֽלֶף
12.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about how many soldiers Abishai and his army killed with the information about what soldiers these were. Alternate translation: [And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomite soldiers in the Valley of Salt]
See how you translated the term “struck” in the similar context in 18:5. Alternate translation: [And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, and his soldiers killed]
The word **Zeruiah** is the name of a woman, David’s older sister.
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:2. Alternate translation: [the Edomites] or [Edomite soldiers]

13.q: וַ⁠יָּ֤שֶׂם בֶּֽ⁠אֱדוֹם֙ נְצִיבִ֔ים וַ⁠יִּהְי֥וּ כָל־אֱד֖וֹם עֲבָדִ֣ים לְ⁠דָוִ֑יד
13.note: It may be more natural in your language to use David’s name in the first instance and a pronoun in the second instance. Alternate translation: [And David put garrisons in Edom, and all of Edom became servants to him]

13.q: וַ⁠יּ֤וֹשַׁע יְהוָה֙ אֶת־דָּוִ֔יד בְּ⁠כֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָלָֽךְ
13.note: After having provided some further details about the plunder David captured, the gifts he received, and how he defeated Edom, the author is once again making a summary comment about everything he has described since introducing a new event in [18:1](ta:18). See how you translated the similar expression in 18:6.

14.note: The phrase **justice and righteousness** expresses a single idea. The word **righteousness** describes what kind of **justice** David carried out. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [he did righteous judgment] or [he decided cases fairly]

15.note: **recorder** was a kind of royal official who kept records of important events and handled official documents. If your readers would not be familiar with what a recorder is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [was the royal secretary] or [was in charge of the official records]

16.note: See how you translated the term “priests” in the similar context in 15:11. Alternate translation: [were the high priests]

17.note: The author is using the image of the **heads** to represent leaders. In this context, the term probably means important officials. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [were important officials]

As in the similar context in 7:29, the author is using the term **hand** to mean “side.” Being at the side of the king represents working closely with the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who were at his side] or [who worked closely with him]
